>Despite all, I have increased my score because I now believe that you bring up interesting points to further understand programmatic policies but the contribution needs to be better framed.

Thank you! We appreciate your engagement. 

Regarding the framing of our work, please refer to our [latest message](https://openreview.net/forum?id=e26MPyczN9&noteId=kNDrLcrOTq).

Thank you for addressing my points!

While I am not an expert in out-of-distribution generalization, I am not convinced by the definition provided in the paper. This is perhaps not surprising, as out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization is notoriously hard to define. However, the term strongly suggests that for OOD, the problem at test time must be in some way structurally different from the training problems—otherwise, it would simply be _in_-distribution generalization. Your definition does not enforce this distinction. Take, for instance, Example 1: A policy could be trained on all graphs, all possible initial nodes, and all possible end nodes except for one. If the policy then generalizes to this one additional end node, your definition would classify this as OOD generalization. I do not believe this definition captures what is usually meant by OOD generalization.

Furthermore, outside the RL domain, OOD generalization of neural networks—especially sequence models—is widely studied, often under the specific name _systematic generalization_. "Generalization without systematicity: On the compositional skills of sequence-to-sequence recurrent networks" (Lake & Baroni, 2017) is often considered a foundational paper in this field.

In general, there are already research programs in place that investigate what algorithms can be represented _in principle_ by different neural network architectures (e.g., "On the Representational Capacity of Recurrent Neural Language Models", Nowak et al., 2024), and what kind of algorithms they learn in practice (e.g., "Neural Networks and the Chomsky Hierarchy", Delétang et al., 2023). It seems to me that the problems encountered in RL OOD generalization are fundamentally the same as those discussed in this literature. I think a stronger version of the paper would take the insights from these research programs and explicitly use them to address OOD generalization in RL.

Finally, regarding the added text: _"These findings suggest that, similarly to how software engineers consider the computational requirements of a problem class when implementing a solution, the choice of which representation to use in RL should consider similar factors..."_

I agree with the sentiment, but this point feels slightly empty. It is arguably a truism that one must choose the right representation and model class for a problem. I would argue that most practitioners are already aware that fixed-capacity models cannot solve problems requiring variable memory (though some papers may indeed overlook this).

summary.value:
This paper presents a re-revaluation of the popular claim that "programmatic policies generalize better than neural network policies". The core thesis is that the previously observed generalization gap stems not from fundamental differences in representation, but largely from experimental confounds.

In this paper, authors revisit three benchmarks (TORC, Karel, Parking). They demonstrate that by applying "minor modifications" to the neural policy learning setup, their out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization can match or even exceed that of programmtic policies.

The paper concludes by using a custom Karel task (learning a stack/queue) to highlight the real benefit of programmatic policies. It argues this advantage is not broad generalization, but the specific, superior ability to execute explicit algorithmic logic.

strengths.value:
1. Directly challenging a widely acknoweledged conclusion and attributing it to "experimental confounds" is a valuable contribution to the community. Researchers are always encouraged to examine and revisit.
2. The effort to re-evaluate three core benchmarks is convincing w.r.t. corresponding algorithms. Concrete experimental evidence (e.g., sparse observations in Karel) to support its central argument: generalization gap stems not from fundamental differences in representation, but largely from experimental confounds. 
3. I am also a bit surprised that slightly tweaking the experimental settings can achive better performance and generalization ability for neural policies. This may be a good lesson for RL researchers that a better formulation of the policy network (even a simple modification) could help the entire experiment.

weaknesses.value:
1. I understand the ambition of this paper but the title seems too "huge". First of all, the claim of programmatic policies generalize better should be explained throughly and more work should be discussed and cited. Programmatic policies are utilized in many other works [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] involving different benchmarks and learning methods. A comprehensive re-evaluation is not realistic and expected, yet discussions are appreciated.
2. I am not fully convinced by the "minor modifications" as tweaking reward function or observation setting are injecting inductive bias, this is not a trivial change to learning of an neural network policy. Also, DSL is a perfect method to inject inductive bias, have you considered tweaking DSL and conduct some experiments? 
3. From my understanding, programatic policies and neural policies are not contradict to each other and can be composed together, this is verified by previous works [1, 6]. Moreover, neural networks are specialized to have better perceptual generalization, yet programmatic policies are suitable for systematic generalization. I believe this aligns many of your research statement, it would be better to discuss this in your revised paper.

[1] Qiu and Zhu, Programmatic Reinforcement Learning without Oracles, ICLR 2022

[2] Cui et al., Reward-guided synthesis of intelligent agents with control structures, PLDI 2024

[3] Kohler et al, Interpretable and Editable Programmatic Tree Policies for Reinforcement Learning, EWRL 2024 Workshop

[4] Guo et al., Efficient Symbolic Policy Learning with Differentiable Symbolic Expression, NeurIPS 2023

[5] Qiu et al., Instructing Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning Agents with Temporal Logic Objectives, NeurIPS 2023

[6] Qureshi et al, Composing Task-Agnostic Policies with Deep Reinforcement Learning, ICLR 2020

Thank you for taking the time to read our revised version and for asking further questions. We have submitted a new version of the paper, as explained below. 

**Comment:** The Python program generated by FunSearch will also run out of memory eventually if presented with problems requiring arbitrarily large memory sizes. 

We agree that any practical implementation ultimately runs on bounded hardware and may exhaust memory if the input grows without limit. Our claim is not that programmatic solutions have infinite memory, but rather that they support policies whose working memory scales with the input instance, whereas the neural policies we evaluate do not. An algorithm whose working memory usage is a function of the input size can generalize to larger instances, whereas a fixed-capacity model cannot. 

An analogy to illustrate the argument is the difference between finite-state machines (FSMs), where the amount of memory is determined at design time, and pushdown automata (PDAs), which can grow their stack according to the input. The latter is strictly more expressive because it can represent nested structures that require unbounded depth; the former cannot. Our argument concerns this property, the ability to grow working memory as a function of the input instance, not infinite hardware.

**Comment:** In this sense I am not sure I fully understand the take home message of Sec. 5.

In addition to the difference between fixing the memory capacity at design time versus allowing it to be a function of the input, as we explained above, we discuss practical issues in Section 5:  

We refer to the work of Joulin & Mikolov (2015) that showed that neural models fail to learn stack-like structures. So even if given enough capacity, it wouldn’t be able to generalize OOD for not learning the underlying data structure needed to solve nested subproblems. In the latest revision, we also added a discussion of the work of Weiss et al. (2018), who showed another example in which the model has enough memory to solve the counting problem of recognizing languages such as $a^nb^n$, but produces imprecise computations and fails to generalize as $n$ grows. A programmatic representation could allow for a pushdown automaton that provably generalizes to arbitrary $n$. 

The take-home message of Section 5 is that OOD generalization depends on the computational requirements of the problem class. We believe bringing computational perspectives from computer science into the study of representations in RL is necessary to understand which representations can generalize OOD.

**Comment:** The new definition of OOD generalization seems also a bit of a tall order, asking solutions to generalize from a single instance to the whole set of problems. 

Thank you for the suggestion. We have softened this definition in the latest version regarding the number of training instances one can use. Here is the updated definition.

> Given a class of problems $(X, F)$, a policy $\pi$ generalizes out of distribution if a learner searches in a policy space $\Pi$ for a policy $\pi$ that solves $F(x)$ for all $x$ in $X_{\text{train}} \subset X$, and the resulting $\pi$ also solves $F(x')$ for any $x'$ in $X$.

We also added a paragraph explaining the practical considerations of this definition to acknowledge that requiring generalization to all instances might be impractical. 

> In practice, $|X_{\text{train}}|$ can be as small as $1$, as in the experiments considered in this paper. Moreover, we often cannot prove that the learned $\pi$ solves all $x'$ in $X$. Instead, we sample $x'$ from a set $X_{\text{test}} \subset X$ with $X_{\text{test}} \cap X_{\text{train}} = \emptyset$ to evaluate a policy's capability of generalizing OOD.

**Comment:** Do you expect every discovered and sufficiently expressive solution of  to generalize to all. 

In practice, a solution does not have to generalize to all instances. As we explained above, one might not be able to prove that a solution generalizes to all instances, but will sample instances from a test set and evaluate them empirically. That way, we can evaluate the extent to which a solution generalizes. 

**Comment:** So what is the formal definition of expressiveness? These concepts currently lack formal definitions.

We added the following two definitions to Section 5.

>[Expressivity] A policy class $\Pi$ is expressive for a problem class $(X, F)$ if there exists a policy $\pi$ in $\Pi$ that generalizes OOD (Definition 1) for $(X, F)$. 

>[Discoverability] Given a policy class $\Pi$ that is expressive for a problem class $(X, F)$, we say that $\Pi$ is discoverable for $(X, F)$ if there exists an algorithm that receives $\Pi$ and $(X, F)$ and returns a policy $\pi$ in $\Pi$ that generalizes OOD for $(X, F)$ within a bounded time limit. 

We use a time bound in the definition of discoverability to make it practical and avoid solutions that trivially enumerate all policies in a class.

summary.value: Good ideas but poor paper. This paper claims that neural network policies transfer better to new tasks w.r.t programmatic policies than previously shown. They claim that poor transferability compared to programmatic policies was the result of cofounding factors in experiments. However this paper itself is poor.

strengths.value: Good number of environments and baselines. Interesting topic.

weaknesses.value:
The most important weakness of this paper is the lack of formalism and rigor.

The claims are not defined and I believe they are tautology. From the abstract ' We argue that a representation enables OOD generalization
if (i) the policy space it induces includes a generalizing policy ', I understand it as: our problem has a solution if there is a solution to our problem.
Similarly, claim (ii) is trivial, 'if an algorithm can find a solution to our problem, our problem has a solution'.

OOD generalization, which is the key metric of this paper is not defined.

Programmatic policies as presented in this paper are mostly non-Markovian, e.g. the programs for the TORCS can query past sensor states in e.g. peek(, -2). This could also be a confounding factor when comparing to Markovian DRL policies.

Authors do not show any convergence curves which is problematic when claiming properties of trained policies.

I don't understand why changing the reward function in the TORCS experiment can explain anything about generalization capabilities of DRL policies. By doing so, you simply changed the problem. In that case you could claim: there exist problems for which DRL policies can generalize as well as programmatic policies. 

I do not understand neither how the other experiments help support the claim that neural network generalize as well or better than programs! what if your training curves did not converge? 

Overall I am not convinced by the problem at hand, the claims, nor the experiments. Key confounding factors include: markovianity of policies (even though it is partially adressed in table 2), potential non-convergence of training, DDPG and PPO were never meant to train policies that generalize OOD so training algorithm choice is also a key confounding factor.

In this sense I am not sure I fully understand the take home message of Sec. 5, and the current modifications do not provide in my opinion any more evidence that the proposed class of problems is particularly suited to programs vs neural nets.

Thank you for your thoughtful review! Your constructive criticism has led us to significantly improve our work. The takeaways you summarized in your review made us realize that we needed to do a better job explaining the insights of our results. Our contributions run much deeper than "programmatic policies are better when the task requires an explicit algorithm", as explained below.  

**Comment:** The learning question in Section 5 seems ill-posed.

**Answer:** Thank you for bringing this up. We agree that the leading questions in Section 5 do not reflect the content of the section. In the revised version, we ask in the title of the section: What does it take to generalize out of distribution? This question accurately reflects the findings presented in the section, which list the properties needed to generalize OOD. 

**Comment:** Clearly, in some environments, programmatic representations generalize better, and in others, neural representations will.

**Answer:** As the reviewer correctly mentioned, perception-based problems such as image recognition are clearly problems for neural networks, so in Section 5, we focus on the question of when neural networks will fail. We then argue that neural policies will fail on problems whose memory requirements grow with the input size. Since the neural models considered in previous work have fixed-size memory, they cannot generalize OOD in problems such as pathfinding, which require a memory capacity that grows with the input size. By contrast, programmatic policies can encode solutions whose memory capacity grows with input size, and can thus generalize OOD. Please see the updated Section 5 for the details. 

**Comment:** it doesn't provide a general framework for identifying these properties in advance in complex, high-dimensional problems (like NetHack, which it mentions ), which would be a more significant contribution. Do the authors have further insights on this?

**Answer:** Following your suggestion, in the revised version, we explain how our findings could help practitioners decide on which representation to use to attain generalization. We added the following paragraph to Section 5:

*These findings suggest that, similarly to how software engineers consider the computational requirements of a problem class when implementing a solution, the choice of which representation to use in RL should consider similar factors, so that the learned policy can attain OOD generalization.*

Then we illustrate with a more detailed example from NetHack (see Section 5).

We hope we have clarified why the conclusions of our work run much deeper than "programmatic policies are better when the task requires an explicit algorithm". To us, both neural and programmatic representations encode explicit algorithms. For example, the wall-following behavior we learned with a feedforward neural network in Karel's Maze is an explicit algorithm. What is important is that this algorithm has a constant memory requirement so that it can be encoded in a feedforward network. The choice of which representation to use is a computational choice. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to raise these questions in the context of representation learning in RL. 

**Question:** Shouldn't the Partially Observable MDP (POMDP) formalism also be introduced for completeness?

**Answer:** We have updated the formalism to POMDPs. Please see Section 2 of the revised version. 

**Comment:** It would significantly improve the paper's clarity and impact to use the expressitvity and discoverability terms consistently from the introduction onwards.

**Answer:** Indeed, the usage of the terms since the introduction improves readability. We have updated the revised version accordingly.

Thank you very much for your feedback! Your suggestions helped us improve our work quite significantly. Please see our detailed comments below. 

**Comment:** The most important weakness of this paper is the lack of formalism and rigor.

**Answer:** Thank you for bringing this up. Indeed, the paper is much easier to follow now that we have formalized OOD generalization and the arguments of when neural representations will fail to enable OOD generalization. In the updated version of the paper, we define a class of problems that allows us to define out-of-distribution generalization as a policy trained on an instance from a problem class that generalizes to all other instances of the same class. Please see the first five paragraphs of Section 2 of the updated version for the details. 

**Comment:** The claims are not defined and I believe they are tautology.

**Answer:** The claims are not tautologies, and we believe this is clear now in the revised version, given the OOD definition we added. 

Let us illustrate with an example to clarify. Consider the class of grid-world problems where an agent lives in a corridor and its goal is to find an opening on the right wall of the corridor. If the problem we train the agent on has an opening on the right after the agent performs 5 steps forward, then the following program can solve it:

*Program 1:*
```python
for _ in range(5):
	forward
turn right
forward
```

However, such a solution does not generalize to other problems in the same class. For example, consider an opening on the wall 3 steps away from the agent. 

A program that would solve any problem in this class is the following:

*Program 2:*
```python
while right-is-blocked:
	forward
turn right
forward
```

Program 2 can solve any problem from this class, regardless of the number of steps forward required; it generalizes OOD. If the policy space doesn't include the Boolean check `right-is-blocked`, then the agent can only find a solution (e.g., Program 1) that does not generalize to other problems in the same class. 

Similarly, claim (ii) isn’t trivial. Consider a policy space that includes Program 1 and Program 2. The search for a solution could be biased toward Program 1, making Program 2 unlikely to be encountered. This is exactly what we observed in some experiments in the literature: neural networks encode generalizable solutions, but gradient descent cannot find them.

**Comment:** OOD generalization, which is the key metric of this paper is not defined.

**Answer:** Thank you for suggesting this. As explained above, we have included the definition of OOD generalization in Definition 1 of the updated version. 

**Comment:** Programmatic policies as presented in this paper are mostly non-Markovian.

**Answer:** This is a great point, and also something we highlight in our paper. For example, we address the non-Markovian nature of Karel by including the last action in the observation space (see Table 1 and Figure 4 of the paper). 

 **Comment:** Authors do not show any convergence curves which is problematic when claiming properties of trained policies.

**Answer:** We have added the learning curves to Appendix E of the revised version. 

**Comment:** Changing the reward function changes the problem.

**Answer:** This is also a great point that needed to be corrected. We clarify in the updated version that the reward we use works as the agent's intrinsic reward function. In the end, the agent is still evaluated on the original reward function, so the problem remains the same. We clarify this in paragraph 3 of Section 4.1 of the updated version.  

**Comment:** I do not understand neither how the other experiments help support the claim that neural network generalize as well or better than programs! what if your training curves did not converge?

**Answer:** We have included the learning curves in Appendix E of the revised version. Having said that, we note that the convergence of the learning curves isn’t important to our argument, as long as we have a systematic way of selecting an output model. For example, LEAPS returns the program with the largest return encountered in search (i.e., at any point of the search). Even if the curves didn't converge, the LEAPS authors presented a systematic and valid way to return the policy to be evaluated in terms of OOD generalization. 

**Comment:** DDPG and PPO were never meant to train policies that generalize OOD so training algorithm choice is also a key confounding factor.

**Answer:** Yes, the assumption that DDPG and PPO cannot produce solutions that generalize is common. In our paper, we show that this assumption does not necessarily hold in practice, and they can indeed find solutions that generalize, after controlling for a few confounding factors.

Thank you for raising all these interesting questions about our work. We would like to clarify your questions below. If not, please let us know. 

**Comment:** In section 5, the author tries to use expressivity and discoverability to define the existence of a generalized solution and a well-developed algorithm for searching the generalized solution. A neural net is a universal function approximator. It is not trivial for a program to have a more generalized solution. Discoverability may be the key advantage for the programmatic policies.

**Answer:** We agree that discoverability could be an advantage of programmatic policies, and this is something future work should exploit. Note, however, that it is not correct to assume that neural networks will always be expressive. Neural networks are indeed universal function approximators, but the key point here is that the models studied are not, in practical terms, Turing complete. In Section 5 of the revised version, we argue that these commonly used neural models cannot accommodate growing memory requirements, such as those needed to solve general pathfinding problems.

**Answer:** A decision tree is sufficient to solve TORCS and Parking. That is why neural networks, which essentially encode a decision tree, should be expressive to solve these problems.

**Answer:** The fully observable baseline is PPO with ConvNet.

The papers we studied claim that programmatic policies generalize better in the specific benchmark problems used in their experiments. That is why we focused on those benchmarks, and, surprisingly, our results show that the conclusions from previous work were incorrect.

**Answer:** Thank you for bringing this up. We performed major improvements to Section 5 of our paper based on your comments.  

Our conclusion that neural networks cannot generalize comes from theory, and not from our experiments. Including experiments with a recurrent model was indeed misleading. Your comments triggered us to remove the neural experiments of Section 5 and argue from a theoretical perspective why networks cannot generalize on general pathfinding problems. The argument we make in the updated Section 5 is simple. Problems such as pathfinding problems can require working memory that grows with the problem input. The neural networks considered have a fixed memory capacity, and for that, they cannot generalize OOD. Please see Section 5 for details. 

**Comment:**  Some of the claim in this paper are perhaps a bit too strong (Sec. 4) are lack supporting evidence (Sec. 5). I would be willing to revise my score if the authors can modulate a bit these claims or provide for instance more evidence on why they believe that neural policies will never be able to generalize to problems in Sec. 5.

**Answer:** Thank you for your comments and suggestions. We have revised the claims in the paper as suggested. In Section 4, we show empirically that modifying the training pipeline enables OOD generalization for neural policies. These claims are fully supported by empirical evidence. We have clarified our claims in Section 5. Instead of saying that neural models cannot generalize on a specific Karel task, we argue that they cannot generalize OOD for the general class of pathfinding problems, which require a growing working memory that these neural models cannot offer. We hope that our answer and the updated version of the paper have addressed your concerns. Please let us know if this is not the case, and we would be happy to clarify.
Despite all, I have increased my score because I now believe that you bring up interesting points to further understand programmatic policies but the contribution needs to be better framed.

**Answer:** While we didn’t spend much time coming up with the changes that we made, we agree we shouldn’t call them minor. We have updated the revised version accordingly to say “a few modifications” instead of “minor modifications”.

**Comment:**  Also, DSL is a perfect method to inject inductive bias, have you considered tweaking DSL and conduct some experiments?

**Answer:** Since the programmatic policies were already shown to generalize OOD in previous work, we focused our experiments on neural models. Having said that, you could see our FunSearch experiment as a way of tweaking a programmatic representation. **Answer:** Yes, the combination of both approaches is a promising (and currently quite active) research direction, which we now discuss in Section 6 of the paper.

summary.value: The paper challenges the idea that neural policies necessarily generalize worse in out-of-distribution scenarios than programmatic policies. To do so, the authors rerun experiments from three existing papers that previously reported better generalization capabilities from programmatic policies and demonstrate that as good out-of-distribution generalization can be obtained by neural policies if one adds a sparsity metric, alters the reward function or changes the inputs given to the neural policies. Finally the paper concludes by modifying one of the (Maze navigation) tasks to make it more challenging  for neural policies and showing that a search algorithm leveraging an LLM can generate a program that solves any kind of such mazes and outperform neural policies trained with PPO.

strengths.value: The paper revisits existing experimental setups and refutes some of their claims or at the very least provides more complete explanations of why neural policies were not generalizing as well in prior experiments.

That a similarly efficient inductive bias can be injected to neural policies by adding a sparsity regularization or by modifying the reward function does not necessarily contradicts the previous statement. It only shows that there are multiple ways of injecting prior information that would help generalization beyond the choice of the policy class. 

Along the same line, I find the experiment in Sec. 5 to be too extreme the other way around: while PPO with a GRU seems to fail to learn a good policy for these Maze problems it does not constitute imo conclusive evidence that neural policies cannot generalize to these type of mazes as stated around line 463. It could very well that the neural architecture was ill-chose or the training procedure could be improved. Especially since the programmatic policies on the other side are trained with a completely different algorithm leveraging much large models. 

Overall, I do like the general direction of the paper. Looking at abstracts of referenced material, prior work do tend to put forth the generalization capabilities of programmatic policies (although it is not always the central claim and interpretability is also discussed prominently), and this paper brings nuance to such claims. In the process however, some of the claim in this paper are perhaps a bit too strong (Sec. 4) are lack supporting evidence (Sec. 5). I would be willing to revise my score if the authors can modulate a bit these claims or provide for instance more evidence on why they believe that neural policies will never be able to generalize to problems in Sec. 5.

summary.value:
The paper re-evaluates the out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization properties of programmatic policies found by different search algorithms (e.g., NDPS, LEAPS, PSM). In previous literature, these policies were often reported to generalize better than neural policies trained with gradient-based methods (e.g., DDPG, PPO, DQN). This paper demonstrates that in several environments (TORCS, Karel, Parking) , straightforward modifications to the neural policy's training allow them to match or exceed the generalization of programmatic policies.

The paper argues that often both neural and programmatic representations can 
*in principle* encode a generalizing policy (a property the paper later calls "Expressivity"). The reported gap in prior work stemmed from "uncontrolled experimental factors" that made finding this solution _in practice_ (a property called "Discoverability") more difficult for the neural policy's search algorithm (i.e., gradient descent). The paper then argues that a true advantage for programmatic policies exists in environments where neural networks struggle to encode generalizing policies even _in principle_. This often involves tasks requiring algorithmic solutions, such as learning specific data structures like a stack or queue. One such environment ("SparseMaze") is shown as a proof-of-concept : a GRU policy trained with PPO fails to learn or generalize, whereas a programmatic policy found by FunSearch discovers a breadth-first search algorithm and provably generalizes.

strengths.value:
- The paper provides a valuable corrective to some claims in the literature about the superior OOD generalization of programmatic policies over neural ones.
- The re-evaluation experiments in TORCS, Karel, and Parking appear sound and clearly demonstrate how the exact experimental setup impacts generalization .
- The distinction between a representation's _expressivity_ (containing a solution) and the _discoverability_ of that solution by a search algorithm can aid further discussion of generalization.

weaknesses.value:
While the paper's re-evaluation of prior work is valuable, its main positive claim feels limited. The paper argues that the _true_ advantage of programmatic policies lies in their _expressivity_ for tasks requiring complex algorithmic structures (like memory or data structures), which common neural network architectures lack .

In my view, this is a well-understood distinction, and the "SparseMaze" proof-of-concept serves more to confirm this known limitation of standard recurrent networks than to provide a new, surprising insight. It would be similarly straightforward to design an environment where neural network policies generalize better (e.g., an environment based on classifying handwritten digits, where the task is perceptual and the underlying "program" is unknown).

The paper wants to guide future evaluation of OOD generalization in RL. However, the main take-away message seems to be "programmatic policies are better when the task requires an explicit algorithm," which is not a particularly novel conclusion. For this reason, the contribution feels limited, which is why I vote for a weak reject.

questions.value:
Below I list more details in the form of questions and comments:
- Section 5 asks the question, "Can programmatic representations better generalize to OOD problems?". This question seems ill-posed, as I have argued above. Clearly, in some environments, programmatic representations generalize better, and in others, neural representations will. More reasonable questions might be: "What are the properties of environments that make programmatic representations more suitable than neural representations, and vice versa? For a given complex environment, how can we determine in advance which kind of representation will generalize better? What representations will generalize better in relevant real-world problems?" The paper _does_ suggest an answer to the first question—that the key property is the need for algorithmic structures like memory manipulation, stacks, or queues. However, it doesn't provide a general framework for identifying these properties in advance in complex, high-dimensional problems (like NetHack, which it mentions ), which would be a more significant contribution. Do the authors have further insights on this?
- In Section 2, the paper formally introduces Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) . However, for the KAREL environment, it explicitly investigates "the partially observable version" and even shows a classic state-aliasing diagram (Figure 4) where different states lead to the same observation. Shouldn't the Partially Observable MDP (POMDP) formalism also be introduced for completeness?
- The paper introduces the core concepts of its argument—that a representation must (i) include a generalizing policy and (ii) the search algorithm must be able to find it—in the abstract and introduction. However, it only formally names these concepts "Expressivity" and "Discoverability" in Section 5 . It would significantly improve the paper's clarity and impact to use these terms consistently from the introduction onwards.

We appreciate your follow-up and address your main comments below.

**Comment:** First, consider more games and classical mdps (mujoco atari ...).

Our work examines claims in the existing literature that programmatic representations outperform neural policies in OOD generalization in specific benchmarks. We are not aware of analogous claims in Atari or MuJoCo. If you are referring to specific works in these domains, we would be grateful for pointers. In the absence of such claims, expanding to those domains would explore a different research question than the one addressed in this paper.

**Comment:** it is too bad that the training curves are not in the main text because they help mitigate the confounding factor of the search algos.

We have added the learning curves to the appendix, which is easily accessible to the reader. 

Importantly, our argument does not rely on the shape of the learning curves. The core claim is that neural representations are capable of OOD generalization on the studied domains. As long as a systematic and reproducible procedure is used to select the final policy (e.g., the final checkpoint or the best-performing checkpoint according to a metric), the central observation remains unchanged. In this context, the learning curves do not reveal or conceal confounds; the conclusion depends on the existence of successful neural policies, not the trajectory of training.

**Comment:** You could use the same search algorithm for dsl and nn policies. Then it would really support whatever you claim from those large scale experiments about the OOD gen. of policies.

There are two ways to interpret this suggestion. Which of the following do you mean? 

1. We should use gradient descent to find programmatic policies.
2. We should train neural networks using discrete search algorithms for program search. 

In both cases, the suggested direction presents difficulties:

For (1): The languages considered in prior work (e.g., the Karel language) can be nondifferentiable. Even when differentiability is available for parts of the policy (e.g., program parameters), the program structure itself is not differentiable. Therefore, gradient descent is not applicable in this setting.

For (2): Neural networks are typically optimized via gradient-based methods because they are efficient and effective. Replacing this with discrete program-search algorithms would introduce additional confounds and depart from standard practice in the literature. This change would obscure, rather than clarify, comparisons of OOD generalization.

**Comment:** forget about this "confounding factor" from previous works that seemed to have bothered other reviewers than me as well. Why not simply write the papaer about inductive biases in RL policies?

We respectfully disagree. Our central contribution is to show that experimental confounds have led to incorrect conclusions about OOD generalization in prior work. We view this clarification as both necessary and impactful for the community, because it directly re-examines widely cited empirical claims.

If by “bothered” you refer to specific reviewer comments, we would appreciate it if you could point us to them. In our reading of the reviews, the other four reviewers explicitly mentioned this contribution as a strength. 

We hope these clarifications are helpful. Thank you again for engaging with our work.

summary.value: The paper re-evaluates the claimed out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization of programmatic policies compared to RL-trained neural policies. The paper attempts to answer what causes the generalizability.. The author conducted their experiment on three domains, TORCS, KAREL, and PARKING. In TORCS, the author modified the reward function to test their hypothesis and show DRL algorithms can generalize to OOD environments. In KAREL, the author utilizes the last action and augmentation for policy training, demonstrating better generalization performance compared to existing baselines. In PARKING, RL shows better performance in training against the programmatic state machine, but has similar performance in the testing stage, showing the poor generalization ability of neural policies. The experimental results show that the programmatic representation and neural representation have similar performance in terms of generalization. The authors designed a new task, SparseMaze in KAREL, and utilized FunSearch to search programmatic policies with a large language model, resulting in better generalization against neural-based policies. Based on the evidence, the authors suggest that future benchmarks should consider the advantages and disadvantages of policy representation.

strengths.value:
1. Recent programmatic reinforcement learning shows out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. The paper shows that with carefully curated training techniques, neural-based policies can also generalize to OOD testing sets.
2. The author proposed a new task called SparseMaze that needs search algorithms to find the target. Using an existing search algorithm can find a solution, whereas PPO cannot find a good policy in the training stage.

weaknesses.value:
1. In section 5, the author tries to use expressivity and discoverability to define the existence of a generalized solution and a well-developed algorithm for searching the generalized solution. A neural net is a universal function approximator. It is not trivial for a program to have a more generalized solution. Discoverability may be the key advantage for the programmatic policies.
2. The advantage of using a data structure is limited to navigation problems like KAREL. For the control problems like TORCS and PARKING, which data structure is needed to solve these problems more generally?
3. The paper discusses some aspects of the generalization. Clearly state each environment's focus on those kinds of generalization. For instance, the PARKING environment discussed the distribution shift generalization, and the KAREL environment discussed the input-scale generalization.
4. Following 3, Liu et al. [1] compose programs in the KAREL environment to solve the tasks with h reward signal. The compositional generalization of policies is not discussed in the paper.

Thank you again for your follow-up. Your clarification helps us better understand your concern, and we address it below.

**Comment:** Previous work did not focus on OOD gen. of NNs while e.g. PIRL (Verma et al) have observed this, it is not a their main claim. 

We agree that OOD generalization was not the central claim of these works. Our motivation is not to dispute their core contributions. We view the cited papers as important and influential, and our own work benefited from them.

However, these works include explicit statements that programmatic policies generalize better than neural ones on the benchmarks they study. These statements have been cited in the literature as evidence of a representational advantage. Our results show that, for these benchmarks, neural policies can also generalize even when trained with only a few modifications. We believe clarifying this point is scientifically valuable, regardless of whether OOD generalization was the primary claim of the original papers.

In research, re-examining secondary or implicit claims can be as informative as revisiting primary ones, particularly when those claims influence how subsequent work is framed.

**Comment:** Hence, it seems far fetched to build your contributiln on refuting something that was not clearly shown.

This is precisely where we see our contribution. The field currently holds the implicit belief that programmatic policies generalize more easily OOD. Our experiments indicate that this belief does not hold for the benchmark domains where the claim originated.

We then go further: we identify conditions under which we do expect programmatic representations to have advantages (e.g., when memory requirements scale with input size). Our intention is to shift the conversation away from representation labels (“programs vs networks”) and toward computational properties that determine whether a policy class can generalize OOD.

**Comment:** And I believe there is on ather reviewer that mentioned that : " I am not sure I completely agree with the claim that previously reported advantages [...]”

Yes, Reviewer nk99 presented a similar view to the one you described. We agree that prior papers did not state that programmatic policies *always* generalize better. What we claim is that, in the domains where the claims were empirically demonstrated, the observed advantages originate from experimental conditions rather than intrinsic representational properties. We have clarified that in our response to Reviewer nk99. 

We would also like to highlight another point made by Reviewer nk99:

> Looking at abstracts of referenced material, prior work do tend to put forth the generalization capabilities of programmatic policies (although it is not always the central claim and interpretability is also discussed prominently), and this paper brings nuance to such claims.

We see our contribution this way: clarifying how and why the observed generalization arises, and providing nuance to prior results by distinguishing between representational power and the experimental conditions under which policies are trained.

summary.value: The primary concerns raised by multiple reviewers are, better OOD generalization of programmatic policies is not a claim but simply an experimental observation, what constitutes minor modifications to NNs, and the experimental evaluation is limited. The authors have attempted to address the concern about OOD generalization not being a primary claim by stating it is a secondary or implicit claim. The discussion around this point revolved around semantics and was weakened by the absence of a definition of OOD generalization in the original version of this paper, and a disagreement about the appropriateness of the proposed definition. The authors did not sufficiently address the concern around what constitutes ‘minor modification’ to NN training, and some reviewers argue that changing the reward function provides another mechanism for injecting prior knowledge into training. Considering NNs are universal function approximators, the fact that a NN can be found to perform as well as the programmatic policy on generalization (or any metric) is well-understood and the paper does not expand our understanding of this phenomenon. The limited experimental evaluation is justified by the authors as necessary since these are the environments used in previous work. However, reviewers assert that additional environments would strengthen the paper’s claims.

reviewer_concerns.value: The primary contribution of the paper is an attempt to challenge the claim of superior OOD generalization of programmatic policies when compared to NNs. The reviewers concerns are two-fold, (i) existing work has not made this claim, only observed generalization in some experiments, and (ii) the fact that modifying the NN or its training is likely to provide better OOD generalization is know and not contested by existing work. The authors have not provided conclusive evidence against these criticisms.

reviewer_scores.value: I do not think the reviewers would have changed their score even if the discussion had continued unimpeded.

Thank you for reading our response and asking further questions, which we address below. 

**Comment:** I am not convinced by the definition provided in the paper [because it does not exclude trivial (non-OOD) cases].

**Answer:** Our definition is not intended to exclude trivial cases, just as the standard definition of POMDP does not exclude trivial environments. Instead, it is intended to define class of problems in which instance complexity can grow or the structural configuration can change. This allows us to speak about algorithmic solutions to classes of problems (e.g., pathfinding on graphs of increasing size), which is central to the evaluation of OOD generalization we discuss.

**Comment:** A policy could be trained on all graphs, all possible initial nodes, and all possible end nodes except for one. If the policy then generalizes to this one additional end node, your definition would classify this as OOD generalization. 

**Answer:** While we don’t intend to have a definition that prevents trivial cases, we want to point out that our pathfinding example is not trivial. One cannot train on all graphs because there is an infinite number of them. The training set can be large, and there will always be graphs that weren’t seen in training (e.g., you can always test on graphs that are larger than those used in training). 

**Comment:**  "Generalization without systematicity: On the compositional skills of sequence-to-sequence recurrent networks" (Lake & Baroni, 2017) is often considered a foundational paper in this field.

**Answer:** Lake & Baroni’s work studies compositionality in supervised sequence learning. Our paper, in contrast, revisits OOD generalization claims from existing RL papers. Since we do not introduce new benchmarks or study compositional generalization in supervised settings, their setting and goals differ from ours, so it falls outside the scope of our analysis.

**Comment:** In general, there are already research programs in place that investigate what algorithms can be represented in principle by different neural network architectures (e.g., Nowak et al., 2024), and what kind of algorithms they learn in practice (e.g., Delétang et al., 2023).

**Answer:** Thank you for referring to Nowak et al.'s and Delétang et al.'s work. Both works highlight a point we already made in Section 5 while citing Weiss et al.: recurrent models are more limited than early theory had pointed out. We have edited Section 5 to also cite these two papers, where previously we only cited Weiss et al.:

> Although recurrent models are, in theory, computationally universal (Siegelmann & Sontag, 1994; 1995), recent work has shown that they are more limited, theoretically (Nowak et al., 2023) and empirically (Delétang et al., 2023). For example, even when the model has the memory capacity required to solve the problem, increasing the memory needed can lead to imprecise computation, as Weiss et al. (2018) showed in their counting experiment: while LSTMs can learn to count so they can recognize languages such as $a^nb^n$, as the value of $n$ grows during test time, the model starts to present what they called a “slightly-imprecise counting” behavior and fail to generalize to large $n$. By contrast, a programmatic representation could implement a pushdown automaton that provably generalizes for any value of $n$.

**Comment:** I think a stronger version of the paper would take the insights from these research programs and explicitly use them to address OOD generalization in RL.

**Answer:** We agree that integrating these research programs to build a comprehensive theory of OOD in RL is an important direction. Our current contribution has a narrower scope: we focus on the re-evaluation of existing OOD claims, and we provide testable insights based on representational capacity. We hope this paper helps inform and motivate deeper investigations of precisely the kind you mention. 

**Comment:** Finally, regarding the added text: "These findings suggest that, similarly to how software engineers consider the computational requirements of a problem class when implementing a solution, the choice of which representation to use in RL should consider similar factors..."[...] is arguably a truism.

**Answer:** Taken in isolation, the quoted sentence may sound like a truism. However, within the context of our Section 5 discussion, this statement highlights a nuance that is not made explicit in the RL literature. Most works motivate the use of recurrent models primarily through partial observability (i.e., if a problem is partially observed, then use a recurrent model). Our examples show that computational requirements such as instance-scaling memory and nested subproblem structure matter independently of observability. By making this connection explicit, we hope to encourage evaluations that align the representation class with the computational demands of the task family.

We sincerely thank all reviewers for their thoughtful and detailed comments. We have revised our paper to address all comments and suggestions received. While we respond to all reviews below, we summarize the major changes in the paper here. All changes in the text are marked in blue. 

1. Added a definition of OOD generalization [nJfM].
2. Added the learning curves to the appendix [nJfM].
3. Rewrote Section 5 to tighten our claims [nk99, 3Ej4, JPvv].
4. Added a related work section [mxig, JPvv].

We look forward to our discussion and to clarifying any further questions you may have.

Best regards,
Authors
We appreciate your review of our response and your updated evaluation.
